tagline: Into Chateau Country on a road once sold for a dollar.
intro: The byway starts at Rodney Square in downtown Wilmington, laid out in the early 1900s by a du Pont man in the City Beautiful spirit, and heads northwest past the downtown high-rises on Routes 52 and 100. Inside a dozen miles the city gives way to the rolling estate land people call Chateau Country.

The water-powered mills of the lower Brandywine built Wilmington, and the du Ponts made their start on its banks. Pierre S. du Pont bought the Kennett Pike itself in 1919, widened and paved it, and sold it to the state for a dollar. The byway ends at the Pennsylvania line by Centreville, a turnpike village named for sitting midway between Wilmington and Kennett Square.

moments.title: Nemours Estate
moments.text: Alfred I. du Pont's 105-room mansion, built to resemble a French chateau as a gift for his wife, keeps among its antiques a clock made for Marie Antoinette, which she never received.

moments.title: Hagley Museum and Library
moments.text: In 1802 E. I. du Pont built powder mills on this bank of the Brandywine, chosen for the creek's tumble over the Fall Line. The powder yards and family home remain.

moments.title: Winterthur
moments.text: Henry Francis du Pont's estate, named by earlier owners for a town in Switzerland, holds one of the richest collections of Americana in the country, and part of its woods is old-growth forest.
